speaker: paulmcleish
text: Okay, good evening, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to this evening's meeting of the Manningham City Council. Begin with item one, the opening prayer and statement of acknowledgement. Almighty God, we pray for your blessing upon this council, help and prosper its work for the advancement and benefit of its people, so that peace and happiness, unity and justice may be established among us all. Amen.

speaker: andrewconlon
text: Amen.

speaker: paulmcleish
text: Manningham City Council acknowledges the Wurundjeri people as the traditional custodians of the land we now know as Manningham. We pay our respects to Wurundjeri elders past and present and value the ongoing contribution to the cultural heritage of Manningham. I'd also like to acknowledge any former councillors and mayors who are attending this evening on the live stream. Council would also like to acknowledge the contribution made to Manningham over the years by people of diverse backgrounds and cultures. I welcome all members of the public to this council meeting and who have joined us online to observe proceedings. In response to the evolving coronavirus situation, changes have been made to the Local Government Act, which permit council meetings to be held virtually for a limited time. The health and safety of our community and employees is our priority during these uncertain times. So we will continue to hold our meetings virtually to further reduce the risk of transmission of COVID-19. You will notice a few changes to how we are conducting our meetings. You will not be able to attend the meeting in person, obviously, however, you are able to watch the meeting via live through the council's website and Facebook page. You can also watch a recording of the meeting at any time afterwards by searching for the meeting on the council website. We are still taking questions from the public and encourage you to submit your questions in accordance with our normal practises prior to the start of the meeting. As you cannot be present in the chamber to read your question, you can elect if you choose to dial in and ask your question, or you may have your question read out by our CEO. A response will be provided where we have the information to hand. If we are unable to provide a meaningful response, we will take your question on notice and provide a response in writing. We will deal with a maximum of two questions per person and two questions on any one issue. If you have more than two questions, please submit these additional questions in writing to council through the normal channels. Finally, I would like to advise that if we experience any technical issues during the meeting, we will make every attempt to resolve them within 30 minutes. If we are unable to resolve the issue, the meeting will be adjourned to another time and date. A notice will be placed on the council's website advising the new meeting date and time and when the adjourned meeting will recommence. Council meetings are governed by Manningham's governance rules. I will introduce each item of business as listed on the agenda, calling it by number and by reading the title. I will then call for a mover and seconder of a motion on the item before opening any debate. Only councillors are able to join the debate on an item. Councillors may adopt the officer's recommendation in the report or propose amendments and supplementary motions. Item two, apologies and requests for leave of absence. I will now confirm the attendance of every councillor. Councillor Mike Zafiropoulos. Present. Councillor Anna Chen.

speaker: paulmcleish
text: Thank you, Mr. Kourambas. Now we have one further question which came in by email. Let me just ask the CEO to read that question. The question comes from Mr. Roland Yu.

speaker: andrewday
text: Thank you, Mayor. In regards to the COVID relief measures, are there any processes or procedures to guarantee local suppliers and residents will have priority for Manningham Council projects and jobs?

speaker: paulmcleish
text: Thank you, Mr. CEO. I'll refer that question to Mr. Philip Lee, Director of Shared Services.

speaker: philiplee
text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. And thank you, Mr. Hu for your question. Whilst we can't guarantee local suppliers and residents will have priority for council's projects, our procurement practices, they're governed by the Local Government Act and we can't favour one supplier over another. However, council's procurement policy and our processes that are in place do encourage council to buy local where possible and where it's feasible. Our procurement framework builds local business into our consideration. And of course, this also depends on local business capacity and capability. Our processes focus on early market research, engagement and analysis, and that also includes a definite focus on local business. Since COVID-19, council has also started to build a local business procurement database.

speaker: mikezafiropoulo
text: Okay, thank you. In May 2020, council endorsed an initial allocation of $300,000 for immediate relief to those in the community who were affected adversely by COVID-19, and in particular, the restrictions that were imposed in our community. Now, this particular report seeks council's consideration for a number of recommendations for the 2020 Community Relief Grants Program. This particular program will fund not-for-profit community groups and directly response to the impacts of COVID-19 pandemic and set in the subsequent lockdowns. So it's not like our community grants. This is directly related to COVID. This particular program has got three categories. The community recovery category. In that category, there were eight applications. The range was between $25,000 and $75,000, and there were two successful applicants who got in total $150,000. The second category is the neighbourhood recovery category. In that category, there were 18 applications. The range was between $10,000 and one to $25,000, and there were eight successful applications totalling more than $130,000. The third category is the grassroots recovery category. The range of that category was between $3,000 and $10,000, and there were 48 applications from the community. 47 of them were successful. It sounds like almost everyone was successful. That is not true because five applications from the previous two categories were transferred to this category. I think it's important to highlight that there was a thorough assessment of those categories by the officers to start with, and then the first two categories were referred to an independent panel. The third category, the grassroots one, was assessed by delegated officers. Now, I think it's important to also mention the sort of groups that benefited from these grants, and these include 22 applications of sporting clubs, 10 community groups, five in the area of arts and learning, 10 in the area of elderly, and five in the area of young people, and five in relation to recreation and health. Now, the sort of needs that those organisations cover are physical activity and sport, mental health, transition to online activities, and this obviously relates to a lot of our elderly, COVID safe activities, arts and events, and food support, which has become an important category for those who are unemployed, elderly, and cannot access food as the rest of us. That's basically it.

speaker: paulmcleish
text: Thank you, Councillor. Are there any speakers against the motion? Are there any other speakers for the motion? Well, Councillors, this is our last financial report as a council before the events that are transpiring in a few weeks time. And I for one am enormously proud of the financial report that we're sending through the government this week. I'll be signing it tomorrow. As was noted, when this council was formed four years, nearly four years ago, we had over $7 million in debt that was inherited by this council for the defined benefit superannuation obligations. We have paid that debt off. Furthermore, we've actually committed a savings programme towards future calls on the defined benefits programme. And we now have cash in reserves put aside for future calls. So we've gone from a council that owed money in respect of this liability to having saved for future purposes. That means we're saving the money as people are employed in those roles, the people that will call on those funds. And that's a very sensible management of the finances of the city. When I look at what we're spending on information technology today, and I compare it where we were four years ago, as a council, it is a light day and night. Four years ago, we were being challenged by the efficacy of our information systems. And we had some challenges in the efficient operation of the council, especially in planning and engineering, because we hadn't had long-term investment in new information technology. We, as a council, adopted a policy of pursuing investment in information technology. We drove cuts in the organisation operating costs to fund that investment in information technology, and we made substantial investments in it. Right across the organisation, we've invested in IT. It's been a substantial enabler of productivity inside the organisation, and it's paid enormous dividends currently in the COVID-19 environment. Because when the council was forced to work from home, we had in place information technology systems that could do it. If this had happened four years ago, our organisation would really have struggled. But when this hit us at the start of this year, we were ready. We had the new phone systems. We had the mobile computers for all the staff. We had portable headsets for the phone system for staff. People could actually take their phone extension from the office, answer it at home, using the council's computer, and continue providing services to our community. That is only as a result of the efforts of this council in funding it, and the extraordinary efforts in the staff of the council in implementing those investments on behalf of the community that have enabled and empowered the organisation to survive in the current environment. And it has delivered an outstanding result in terms of planning performance. speaker: paulmcleish
text: Councillor, our budget was struck with a $12.6 million surplus. And that budget is prepared in compliance with accounting standards. And those accounting standards determine how various items are treated, whether items are treated before surplus or after surplus. And in that surplus of $12.6 million, there are three notable items that are essentially non-cash items. So there is $6.9 million of contributions from developers. So they're developers who are developing property in our city, and I'll talk a little more about that later. Those funds are placed in a special reserve. They can only be used for specific purposes, such as investing in our parks and open spaces. So that had to be included in that 12.6, but it's a payment by developers for future investment in public open space and other matters. There was a $1 million non-monetary contribution, such as assets that are transferred to us. So when a property is developed and they build a stormwater drain or a footpath, or those sorts of things as part of the development, a million dollars of assets transfer to us, and that forms part of that 12.6 million. And the final one is a $2.8 million of payment of capital grants from governments. So those payments of capital grants are specifically for capital works, and they must be treated as a part of the surplus contribution. So all up that comes to about $10.7 million of that 12.6 million is already committed in those three ways that I described. And for accounting reasons, it must be treated as a surplus. But the fact is that it's not actually surplus funds available for council to invest for the community. So when it comes down to the actual underlying cash surplus, it's $1.9 million is our cash surplus. Now, if you look at that, that's in the context of us actually putting $3 million into COVID release in the next 12 months. So, you know, with that $3 million pretty quickly deals with the $1.9 million surplus. But the reality is that the way surpluses are treated from an accounting perspective, that $1.9 million is council is required to contribute those to our reserves. And we then draw on reserves to help fund our capital investment projects. So in the current year, year's budget, we have a $49.9, $50 million capital works program. And we will draw, to fund that $50 million, we will draw $32 million from rates, and we will draw $9.7 million from reserves and developer contributions. So we're putting $1.9 million into the reserves through the surplus, and then we're pulling, and we're putting $6.9 from developer contributions, and then we're pulling $9.7 million from reserves to fund the capital, partly fund the capital works program. So part of the problem, Councillor, is that people are trying to simplify what are the complex accounting arrangements for a council. And that you can't simplify council finances down to one simple headline number and say, you understand it, and that surplus is a terrible thing. It actually comes down to understanding the complex sequence of funds coming in, surplus is going to reserves, reserves being drawn down upon to fund capital works. And that's what we've done. So our capital works program gets 32 million from rates, 9.7 from reserves, 2.8 from external grants, 400,000 from asset sales, and $5 million carried forward from last financial year to complete projects that haven't yet finished. That's where the $50 million in capital works comes from.

speaker: paulmcleish
text: Well, the answer is that we are spending more on our community relief package than we are raising through the rate increase. So we're actually investing more. And the rationale is that our primary source of income is rates. $36 per rateable property or business is a relatively modest increase. It's 2%, it is a modest increase, and it distributes affordability right across our community. It's the only mechanism that we have it's the only mechanism we have essentially to distribute that affordably. And what we have then done is implemented a set of targeted measures to then provide relief in our community to those most in need. So we've set up special payment arrangements for those experiencing financial hardship. We have increased the low income rate rebate by 56%. For those who are on a fixed and very low income, they're able to apply for a rate rebate. We've provided a range of additional support services for all the residents you heard just before from Councillor Chen about over $300,000 going into relief proposals for elderly citizens. We've got the introduction of the Community Relief Fund where there is a million dollars in grants being made available to our community. And earlier this evening, we put $554,000 of that into action, back into our community, providing support for our community as we come out of the COVID lockdown to encourage and reinvigorate our community and provide support in very many ways, such as food relief. One of the grants goes directly to food relief. We've provided, as we heard earlier, over half a million dollars so far, and there's another wave of support going into rent relief and for sporting clubs and community organisations and to social support organisations. There is more going in over the next six months. And we have put a range of relief measures on the table for small business discounts, as we heard earlier in the previous motion. So there's an extensive array of community support targeted at those who are most in need in our community. And that is funded by a modest tax right across the community of $36 per annum, per ratepayer or ratepaying business or household.

And we have maintained our investment. We've maintained our Capital Works Programme. And there's various, one of the reasons we have maintained our Capital Works Programme is that preserves employment and business activity. And if there's one thing we know about at the moment is that business is pulling back on investment, on capital investment. They're pulling back on spending and they're expected to pull back over the next 12 months. And that leads it to government to invest in infrastructure and invest in economic activity in Australia. And all levels of government are investing in economic activity. It's one of the foundation elements of why we as a council decided to proceed with the rate rise and then proceed with the Capital Works Programme, because that economic activity is critical to business. Us spending $49.9 million on Capital Works mean businesses are going to hire staff, purchase materials, build assets for our community, invest in the future of our community and create employment in doing so. And we have a responsibility as a level of government to invest in our community and invest in the employment that flows from that, especially so in an economic recession when businesses are not able to and when there is a severe economic downturn. So I think our decision to proceed with the rate rise was a prudent investment on the behalf of and for the benefit of our community. Thank you. You are most welcome. Councillor Kleinert.
